I hate this argument, and this is why:

While it is definitely a fallacy to assume every pirated song would have been purchased otherwise, it's also a fallacy to assume that all pirated copies would never have been sales if the ability to pirate wasn't present. You can't argue one way and completely invalidate the other regardless of the direction of your argument. Absolutes simply can not, and do not work in this case.

The truth is somewhere in the middle. Some people who pirate would have spent money if they had to, and some would not have spent money under any circumstance. We need to stop with this black and white "all people are the same" mentality. It simply doesn't exist in reality.

The problem is that it's impossible to tell how much of each type exist in the bought vs the would not have bought camps. As such the deck is always stacked against the content creators when arguing if they were actually damaged by piracy.

I see where you are coming from, and I think the pros and cons of piracy, or lets plays, vary from product to product. Nobody doubts that if a product is good enough, piracy, and certainly lets plays, are just free advertising that can drive record sales.

But for certain genres of game, or games that just barely meet a standard of quality, it is not in their best interest for people to play or watch them before purchasing. And I think a lot of publishers saw this back when demos and shareware were more common. Demos actually decreased sales since people would play a demo and be satisfied. Games were far more profitable when publishers could stoke your hype boner for 3 to 6 months, and then the only way to get release was to buy the game immediately.

However, while those sales practices of getting people to purchase games blind and weakly informed is good for a publishers profits, is it really fair to the consumer?

Circling back around to Lets Plays of Walking Simulators, I think a good case study is the backlash against Gone Home. It got hyped to hell and back, and then when people jumped straight into it, they felt incredibly let down and lied to. I'm sure it sold better thanks to Lets Plays being less of a thing at the time. But how many of those sales do you think people regretted? I'd say That Dragon Cancer without lets plays, and with only the gaming press hype behind it would have been a very similar situation. Maybe they would have made more money (or maybe not since Gone Home probably benefited from the lack of a Steam Refund policy), but they'd also have a lot of bitter angry customers.

Edit: Now that I'm no longer on mobile, I'd like to try to quantify the backlash I think Gone Home has received. On Metacritic, it has about a 9 from reviewers but a 5 from anons. That Dragon Cancer by comparison has about an 8 from reviewers, and a 6 from anons. One way to interpret this is that That Dragon Cancer did a better job of finding an audience that appreciates it, with fewer sales to people who weren't properly informed about what they were getting.

Naturally there are other possible conclusions that could be drawn.

Nobody doubts that if a product is good enough, piracy, and certainly lets plays, are just free advertising that can drive record sales.

I am skeptical of this, not because I think it's impossible that it could be true, but because there's simply no reasonable way to quantify it. How do I determine what percentage of piracy attributes itself to advertising that translates in to revenue? Is there an amount of piracy where the returns are considered diminishing? In simplest terms - what amount of piracy is helpful, and when does it become harmful?

It could just be that I'm not aware of the mathematical model that best determines this, but it could also be that it's pretty random since it is dependent on the whims of the consumer, or non-consumer depending on the camp. What I can say is that directly asking consumers doesn't seem like it would get you honest answers.

I probably shouldn't have even mentioned piracy because it's a bit of a red herring in a conversation about Lets Plays weakening sales. And as for Lets Plays, their effect on sales is well documented, at least among certain people in the community. If I recall the correlated sales figures correctly, PewDiePie doesn't drive too many sales relative to his viewership, but people like Game Grumps definitely do.

This isn't something we should be overlooking and saying, "oh well, devs should just keep this in mind and make their games Youtuber-proof." This is something we should be addressing with Youtubers and encouraging them to be more thoughtful of the impact they have on certain specific types of games. If the game is basically a story told through a game engine with little/no actual gameplay, Youtubers shouldn't be posting the entire game for people to see without supporting the developer in any way.

If said developer is not happy with the situation, laws already exist to cover that sort of thing. He can go to court anytime.

It is the responsibility of the developers and publishers to extract revenue from their products, not of anybody else. This isn't high school, you don't get points for effort. Looking at this from a business perspective, I think they're being silly. Let's consider a tuber, their viewers, and how this intersects with your market.

  • Customer 1: Wouldn't have bought your game before watching the tuber, and won't buy it afterwards.
  • Customer 2: Wouldn't have bought your game before watching the tuber, decided to buy it afterwards.
  • Customer 3: Would have bought your game before watching the tuber, but won't buy it afterwards.
  • Customer 4: Would have bought your game before watching the tuber and after.

The only customer that's having a net loss on you is #3. Every single other customer is revenue neutral to revenue positive.

So how can we begin to ballpark the sizes of these numbers? Well in this case it's pretty easy. The game is another walking simulator and people know what they're getting in these sort of games: a mostly noninteractive story experience with no replayability or meaningful gameplay. So how many of these people, who actually planned on purchasing the game to experience for themselves would go to YouTube and start watching let's plays? I think it's extremely safe to say very very few. I think the vast majority of the viewers are going to be people have who never heard of your game or have no idea what it's about, and people who know what it is and have no intentions of purchasing it - and those are all neutral to positive revenue sources for you that that tuber is bringing to you.

If you make games that are all story and little gameplay, you end up with youtube videos being just as good as the game itself. And how do you stop that? What is even the point of buying a game like this, when you only play it for the story and you can get the story from just watching a video? You don't get the same experience watching Let's Plays of Smash Bros, Pokemon, Dark Souls, DriveClub/Forza/etc, CoD, etc. as you do actually playing the game, but in a situation like this movie-game, you get an extremely similar experience.

This is a fundamental problem with targeting the market that's "casual" and doesn't like game play. No one feels compelled to buy the game, because you can just watch videos online and get nearly the same experience. And traditional games don't suffer from that. These movie-games are always going to suffer from this problem, and there's not going to be any stopping it.

This clique of people wanted to turn video games into interactive video. And they're learning that the interactivity they tack as an afterthought doesn't really separate it enough from an actual movie or short film. I suspect this is going to be the new thing for these types of games, and rightly so. Why spend money to watch interactive movies when you can just watch it on youtube?
